claims.text: What the strip looks like An irregularly irreg rhythm w ⍉discernible P waves — a chaotic fibrillatory baseline — and a var ventricular response.
claims.quote: Irregularly irregular rhythm No discernible P waves — chaotic ﬁbrillatory baseline Variable ventricular response

claims.text: Aspects (abnorm in red) Rate: most commonly about 110–160
claims.quote: AF is most commonly associated with a ventricular rate ~ 110 – 160

claims.text: Rapid ventricular response: rate > 100; “slow” AF: rate < 60
claims.quote: AF is often described as having ‘rapid ventricular response’ once the ventricular rate is > 100 bpm. ‘Slow’ AF is a term often used to describe AF with a ventricular rate < 60 bpm.

claims.text: Rhythm: irregularly irreg
claims.quote: Irregularly irregular rhythm

claims.text: P waves: none
claims.quote: No P waves

claims.text: Baseline: ⍉isoelectric baseline
claims.quote: Absence of an isoelectric baseline

claims.text: Fibrillatory waves: may be present — fine (< 0.5 mm) or coarse (> 0.5 mm); they can mimic P waves and lead to misdiagnosis
claims.quote: Fibrillatory waves may be present and can be either fine (amplitude < 0.5mm) or coarse (amplitude > 0.5mm) Fibrillatory waves may mimic P waves leading to misdiagnosis

claims.text: f waves: irreg in timing and shape, @ > 300/min, USU best seen in V1 and ⍉always visible in every lead
claims.quote: Presence of f (fibrillatory) waves between QRS complexes; f waves are irregular in timing and irregular in morphology; baseline undulations at rates > 300 beats/minute, usually best seen in lead V1 and not always apparent in all leads

claims.text: QRS: USU < 120 ms unless there = a pre-existing bundle branch block, an accessory pathway, or rate-related aberrant conduction
claims.quote: QRS complexes usually < 120ms, unless pre-existing bundle branch block, accessory pathway, or rate-related aberrant conduction

claims.text: Ashman phenomenon: a short R-R after a long R-R can give an aberrant beat, typically RBBB-shaped, that mimics a PVC or VT
claims.quote: Atrial fibrillation may also cause a phenomenon that mimics ventricular extrasystoles or ventricular tachycardia (Ashman phenomenon). This phenomenon typically occurs when a short R-R interval follows a long R-R interval; the longer interval lengthens the refractory period of the infra-Hisian conduction system, and the subsequent short R-R QRS complex(es) are conducted aberrantly, typically with right bundle branch morphology

claims.text: Mimic: musc tremor or electrical interference can resemble f waves, but the underlying ventricular rhythm = regular
claims.quote: Muscle tremor or electrical interference may resemble f waves, but the underlying ventricular rhythm is regular.

claims.text: → (mech and diagnoses) Mech: needs an initiating event (focal atrial activity / PACs) and a substrate that maintains it (ex, a dilated Lt atrium)
claims.quote: it requires an initiating event (focal atrial activity / PACs) and substrate for maintenance (i.e. dilated left atrium)

claims.text: Focal activate: AF starts from a focus of ↑automaticity or μ re-entry, often in the pulm veins
claims.quote: Focal activation – in which AF originates from an area of focal activity. This activity may be triggered due to increased automaticity or from micro re-entry. Often located in the pulmonary veins.

claims.text: MCCs: HTN, CAD, cardiomyopathy, valvular dz (MS, MR, TR), hyperthyroidism, binge drinking (“holiday heart”)
claims.quote: The most common causes of atrial fibrillation are Hypertension Coronary artery disease Cardiomyopathy Valvular heart disorders: mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation, tricuspid regurgitation Hyperthyroidism Binge alcohol drinking (holiday heart)

claims.text: Less common Eti: PE, ASD and other congenital ♡ defects, COPD, sleep apnea, myocarditis, pericarditis
claims.quote: Less common causes of atrial fibrillation include Pulmonary embolism Atrial septal defects and other congenital heart defects Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) Sleep apnea Myocarditis Pericarditis

claims.text: Also: acute infections, lyte disturb (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia), thyrotoxicosis, drugs (ex, sympathomimetics), EToH, pulm Emb, pericardial dz, acid-base disturb, pre-excitation syndromes
claims.quote: Acute infections Electrolyte disturbance (hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia) Thyrotoxicosis Drugs (e.g. sympathomimetics) Alcohol Pulmonary embolus Pericardial disease Acid-base disturbance Pre-excitation syndromes

claims.text: Slow AF: hypothermia, digoxin toxicity, meds
claims.quote: Causes of ‘slow’ AF include hypothermia, digoxin toxicity, and medications.

claims.text: CVA risk: ⍉atrial contract lets thrombi form; AF → about 20–25% of all CVAs
claims.quote: The absent atrial contractions predispose to thrombus formation; the overall annual risk of cerebrovascular embolic events is 3 to 5%, and atrial fibrillation is responsible for approximately 20 to 25% of all strokes

claims.text: Sx Often aSx; many have palpitations, chest discomfort, or heart-failure Sx (weakness, light-headedness, dyspnea), particularly when the ventricular rate = very rapid
claims.quote: Atrial fibrillation is often asymptomatic, but many patients have palpitations, chest discomfort, or symptoms of heart failure (eg, weakness, light-headedness, dyspnea), particularly when the ventricular rate is very rapid

claims.text: May present w an acute CVA or other organ damage from systemic emboli
claims.quote: Patients may also present with symptoms and signs of acute stroke or of other organ damage due to systemic emboli.

claims.text: Exam: irregularly irreg pulse, loss of a waves in the JVP; a pulse deficit (apical rate faster than the wrist rate) may be present
claims.quote: The pulse is irregularly irregular with loss of a waves in the jugular venous pulse. A pulse deficit (the apical ventricular rate is faster than the rate palpated at the wrist) may be present

claims.text: Tx Once Eti are managed: ventricular rate control, rhythm control, and prev of thromboembolism
claims.quote: Once causes have been managed, treatment of atrial fibrillation focuses on ventricular rate control, rhythm control, and prevention of thromboembolism.

claims.text: Rate control: all pts, typically to < 100 @ rest
claims.quote: Patients with atrial fibrillation of any duration require rate control (typically to < 100 beats/minute at rest)

claims.text: Rate-control drugs: BBs (ex, metoprolol, esmolol), preferred if excess catecholamines are sus (ex, thyroid disorders, exercise-triggered cases); nondihydropyridine CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem); digoxin = least effective but may be preferred in HF
claims.quote: Beta-blockers (eg, metoprolol, esmolol) are preferred if excess catecholamines are suspected (eg, in thyroid disorders, exercise-triggered cases) (1). Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (eg, verapamil, diltiazem) are also effective. Digoxin is the least effective but may be preferred if heart failure is present.

claims.text: Do ⍉give AV node blockers in WPW w an accessory pathway (wide QRS) — they can increase conduction down the bypass tract and cause VF
claims.quote: CAUTION: AV node blockers should not be used in patients with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome when an accessory AV pathway is involved (indicated by wide QRS duration); these medications may increase frequency of conduction via the bypass tract, possibly causing ventricular fibrillation

claims.text: New-onset AF causing HF or hemodynamic compromise: restore sinus rhythm
claims.quote: In patients with heart failure or other hemodynamic compromise directly attributable to new-onset atrial fibrillation, restoration of normal sinus rhythm is indicated to improve cardiac output

claims.text: Acute conversion: synchronized cardioversion or meds
claims.quote: For acute conversion, synchronized cardioversion or medications can be used.

claims.text: B4 conversion: control the rate to < 120 and anticoagulate most pts — any conversion transiently raises thromboembolic risk
claims.quote: Before conversion is attempted, the ventricular rate should be controlled to < 120 beats/minute, and most patients should be anticoagulated (for criteria and methods, see Prevention of thromboembolism) because conversion of atrial fibrillation, regardless of the method used, transiently increases the risk of thromboembolism.

claims.text: Anticoagulation: weigh CVA risk against bleed risk, using RF or a score such as CHADS2 or CHA2DS2-VASc
claims.quote: Anticoagulation guidelines are based on risk of stroke vs. risk of bleeding. Stroke risk stratification requires either an assessment of risk factors or application of a risk score e.g. CHADS2 or CHA2DS2VASc.

claims.text: Paroxysmal AF lasting > 48 hrs = unlikely to revert on its own — consider anticoagulation
claims.quote: Note paroxysmal AF of > 48 hr duration is unlikely to spontaneously revert to sinus rhythm and anticoagulation must be considered.
